# A realistic corn pipeline: AlphaSimR and reciprocal recurrent selection {#sec-alphasimr} @sec-simulating-crosses built the `{X, f, hybrids, fL}` contract with a deliberately fast simulator: Balding-Nichols allele frequencies, independent markers, no recombination, no dominance. That is enough to exercise the diversity and selection machinery, but it is not how a two-heterotic-pool corn programme is actually run. This chapter reproduces the real method -- **reciprocal recurrent selection** (RRS; @comstock1949) -- with AlphaSimR's founder-haplotype and meiosis engine (@gaynor2021), and shows that the same contract comes out the other end, unchanged, so `stage2_select()` runs on it exactly as it does on the book's own simulated data. RRS is the standard commercial scheme for two heterotic pools: each pool is improved using the *other* pool as tester. Doubled-haploid lines are drawn from pool A, testcrossed to pool B (and vice versa), the testcross hybrids are phenotyped, and the lines with the best mean testcross performance -- a proxy for general combining ability, GCA -- are recombined to found the next cycle's pool. Elite lines from both pools, at the end, are crossed directly to produce the commercial hybrids. It is exactly the asymmetry @sec-cycles argues for: selection happens on the hybrid, recycling happens within pool. The engine lives in the package, `R/13_alphasimr_bridge.R`: `rrs_config`, `alphasimr_founder_pools()`, `alphasimr_rrs_cycle()`, `alphasimr_make_hybrids()` and `alphasimr_to_stage1()`, wrapped by `alphasimr_pipeline()`. AlphaSimR is a `Suggests` dependency, guarded exactly like `quadprog` and `highs` elsewhere in the package -- this chapter, and only this chapter, needs it. ## Founding two pools with a real coalescent history `AlphaSimR::runMacs2(..., split = )` draws founder haplotypes from a population-split coalescent history: one ancestral population, then two demes diverging `split` generations ago. That is the realistic analogue of `simulate_lines()`'s Balding-Nichols draw in @sec-simulating-crosses, and it comes with what the book's own simulator cannot give: actual linkage and recombination. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fp <- alphasimr_founder_pools(rrs_cfg) c(pool_A = fp$pop_A@nInd, pool_B = fp$pop_B@nInd, markers = rrs_cfg$n_chr * rrs_cfg$seg_sites) #> pool_A pool_B markers #> 12 12 750 alphasimr_gd(fp$pop_A, fp$SP) #> [1] 0.222838 alphasimr_gd(fp$pop_B, fp$SP) #> [1] 0.2273519 ``` ::: `alphasimr_gd()` is `1 - mean(f)`, the exact definition `gene_diversity()` uses, computed directly from AlphaSimR's genotype pull -- so the two pools are already comparable to every diversity number in the rest of the book on the same scale. Each pool also carries an additive-and-dominance trait (`SP$addTraitAD(meanDD = 0.4, varDD = 0.1)`). Dominance is what makes testcross selection meaningful at all: without it, a line's performance in cross would just be its own breeding value, and there would be nothing for RRS to exploit that plain within-pool selection could not already get. @sec-heterosis covers why dominance is the mechanism. ## One cycle ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cy1 <- alphasimr_rrs_cycle(fp$pop_A, fp$pop_B, fp$SP, rrs_cfg) fmt(cy1$summary, 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| mean_tc_A| mean_tc_B| gd_A| gd_B| |---------:|---------:|------:|------:| | 1.4613| 2.134| 0.1816| 0.1918|
::: ::: `alphasimr_rrs_cycle()` draws 3 doubled-haploid lines per parent in each pool, testcrosses them to 2 individuals from the *other* pool, phenotypes the testcrosses, keeps the 6 lines per pool with the best mean testcross phenotype, and recombines them (`randCross()`) to found the next cycle's pool. `elite_A`/`elite_B` in its return value are exactly the lines that survive, kept for the final cross. ## The trajectory across cycles ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} res <- alphasimr_pipeline(rrs_cfg) fmt(res$cycles, 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| cycle| mean_tc_A| mean_tc_B| gd_A| gd_B| |-----:|---------:|---------:|------:|------:| | 1| 2.2771| 1.8459| 0.1745| 0.1701| | 2| 2.8413| 2.9692| 0.1489| 0.1459| | 3| 3.7390| 3.8784| 0.1233| 0.1199| | 4| 4.7097| 4.2006| 0.1036| 0.0837|
::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Reciprocal recurrent selection over four cycles, book scale. Left: mean testcross phenotype (selection response) per pool. Right: gene diversity of the elite lines retained each cycle.](04c-alphasimr-pipeline_files/figure-html/fig-alphasimr-cycles-1.png){#fig-alphasimr-cycles fig-align='center' width=1350} ::: ::: Both pools respond -- mean testcross phenotype rises -- and both pools lose gene diversity in their retained elite lines, cycle over cycle. Nobody pays this cost for its own sake: @sec-cycles makes the same point with the package's own faster simulator, over a longer trajectory and a grid of selection intensities. This chapter shows it holds with actual meiosis and dominance behind it too. ## The final hybrid pool through `stage2_select()`, unchanged ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} st1 <- res$stage1 dim(st1$X) #> [1] 36 750 sel <- stage2_select(st1$X, st1$f, st1$hybrids, n_sel = 8, fL = st1$fL) #> [1/4] null distribution by resampling (B = 2000 cheap, 200 full)... #> GD reference = 0.22708 (sd 0.00376) #> Monte-Carlo s.e. 8.4e-05 -> alpha differences below 0.037% are noise #> bias if using the population as reference: 2.02% #> [2/4] maximum attainable alpha (pure truncation) = 0.47% #> [3/4] warm start (greedy) and DE per scenario... #> DE_alpha_0.00 index 1.298 | alpha achieved -1.675% | Ns 0.6501 | Ne_par 9.1 #> DE_alpha_0.12 index 1.349 | alpha achieved 0.054% | Ns 0.6468 | Ne_par 9.1 #> DE_alpha_0.24 index 1.351 | alpha achieved 0.220% | Ns 0.6465 | Ne_par 9.1 #> DE_alpha_0.35 index 1.351 | alpha achieved 0.220% | Ns 0.6465 | Ne_par 9.1 #> DE_alpha_0.47 index 1.375 | alpha achieved 0.472% | Ns 0.6460 | Ne_par 9.8 #> [4/4] metrics per scenario... #> F_hom is what the constraint pins; F_drift is what it does not: #> DE_alpha_0.00 F_hom +0.0031 | F_drift 0.0161 | gap -0.0130 | GD_BS 0.1434 #> DE_alpha_0.12 F_hom +0.0352 | F_drift 0.0263 | gap +0.0089 | GD_BS 0.1462 #> DE_alpha_0.24 F_hom +0.0457 | F_drift 0.0229 | gap +0.0228 | GD_BS 0.1470 #> DE_alpha_0.35 F_hom +0.0457 | F_drift 0.0229 | gap +0.0228 | GD_BS 0.1470 #> DE_alpha_0.47 F_hom +0.0507 | F_drift 0.0202 | gap +0.0305 | GD_BS 0.1453 #> ref_truncation F_hom +0.0507 | F_drift 0.0202 | gap +0.0305 | GD_BS 0.1453 #> ref_trunc_cap F_hom +0.0507 | F_drift 0.0202 | gap +0.0305 | GD_BS 0.1453 #> ref_max_div F_hom -0.0458 | F_drift 0.0121 | gap -0.0579 | GD_BS 0.1376 #> ref_random F_hom +0.0935 | F_drift 0.0293 | gap +0.0642 | GD_BS 0.1498 fmt(sel$metrics[, c("scenario", "alpha", "GD", "GD_BS", "F_ST", "index")], 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|scenario | alpha| GD| GD_BS| F_ST| index| |:--------------|-------:|------:|------:|------:|-------:| |DE_alpha_0.00 | -0.0167| 0.2309| 0.1434| 0.6211| 1.2979| |DE_alpha_0.12 | 0.0005| 0.2270| 0.1462| 0.6440| 1.3488| |DE_alpha_0.24 | 0.0022| 0.2266| 0.1470| 0.6486| 1.3515| |DE_alpha_0.35 | 0.0022| 0.2266| 0.1470| 0.6486| 1.3515| |DE_alpha_0.47 | 0.0047| 0.2260| 0.1453| 0.6430| 1.3752| |ref_truncation | 0.0047| 0.2260| 0.1453| 0.6430| 1.3752| |ref_trunc_cap | 0.0047| 0.2260| 0.1453| 0.6430| 1.3752| |ref_max_div | -0.0356| 0.2352| 0.1376| 0.5850| -0.2180| |ref_random | 0.0267| 0.2210| 0.1498| 0.6776| 0.0619|
::: ::: Nothing here is AlphaSimR-specific: `stage2_select()` never sees where `X`, `f`, `hybrids` and `fL` came from, only that they satisfy the contract stage 1 promises. `GD_BS`, the between-pool divergence that carries the heterosis signal (@sec-choosing), is computed from `fL` exactly as it is everywhere else in the book. ## Assumptions, and what this adds over @sec-simulating-crosses **What is more realistic here.** Actual recombination and linkage (a genetic map per chromosome, not independent markers), a dominance-driven trait so testcross selection has something real to select on, and multi-generation recurrent selection rather than one static pool. **What is still simplified.** Testers are a small fixed subset of the opposite pool (2 individuals), not a full single- or multi-location trial; there is one phenotyping environment (`setPheno()`'s error variance, no genotype-by-environment term); the population-split coalescent history (`runMacs2(split = )`) is a stylised divergence process, not calibrated to a named heterotic-pool pair; and doubled-haploid production is instantaneous, skipping the field seasons a real DH pipeline takes. **Scale.** This chapter runs live at a book scale (12 + 12 founders, 750 markers, 4 cycles) -- AlphaSimR is fast enough at this size that no caching is needed, unlike the MABC scans in @sec-backcross. A heavier, production-scale run is `inst/scripts/run_alphasimr.R`: ```sh Rscript inst/scripts/run_alphasimr.R --test # smoke run, ~10 s Rscript inst/scripts/run_alphasimr.R --out=DIR # full run, ~2 min ``` It runs `alphasimr_pipeline()` at a larger configuration, feeds the resulting hybrid pool through `stage2_select()`, and writes the cycle trajectory and selection metrics as CSVs. ## Where this connects @sec-simulating-crosses and this chapter build the same three-object contract from two different generative models -- the fast one and the realistic one -- which is the point of drawing that seam where the book does: everything past it, `build_ctx()` through `stage2_select()`, cannot tell which one it is looking at. @sec-heterosis explains why the dominance term here is what makes testcross selection informative at all. @sec-cycles runs the same diversity-erosion argument at a longer horizon with the package's own faster simulator; this chapter is its cross-check against an engine with real meiosis behind it.
